binders: A finite Poisson parameter λ (PDF page 6, printed page 10; anchors: the preceding Poisson definition and the limit ∑_i p_{N,i} → λ).

For every positive integer N, Bernoulli random variables X_{N,1}, ..., X_{N,N} and their parameters p_{N,1}, ..., p_{N,N} (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: independent Bernoulli random variables with parameters p_{N,i}).
The row sums S_N := ∑_{i=1}^N X_{N,i} (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: the sum whose Poisson convergence is asserted).
hypotheses: Within each N-th row, X_{N,1}, ..., X_{N,N} are independent (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: independent Bernoulli random variables).

Each X_{N,i} has Bernoulli parameter p_{N,i}, hence takes the Bernoulli success/failure values with the indicated success probability (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: Bernoulli random variables with parameters p_{N,i}).
As N tends to infinity, max_{1≤i≤N} p_{N,i} tends to 0 (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: the first displayed limiting assumption).
As N tends to infinity, ∑_{i=1}^N p_{N,i} tends to the finite parameter λ (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: the second displayed limiting assumption).
conclusions: As N tends to infinity, S_N = ∑_{i=1}^N X_{N,i} converges in distribution to the Poisson distribution with parameter λ (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Section 1.3, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: the theorem's concluding Poisson-convergence assertion).
definitions_and_conventions: A Poisson random variable with parameter λ has probability mass P{Z=k}=e^{-λ}λ^k/k! for k=0,1,2,... (PDF page 6, printed page 10; anchor: the Poisson definition immediately preceding Theorem 1.3.4).

A Bernoulli variable with parameter p_{N,i} is the two-point success/failure variable associated with that probability; this model identity is part of the theorem's premise, not replaceable merely by matching its mean and variance (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: Bernoulli random variables with parameters p_{N,i}).
The index N selects a row and i ranges from 1 through N within that row (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; structural anchor: X_{N,1}, ..., X_{N,N}).
The convergence arrow in the conclusion denotes convergence in distribution (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: converges in distribution).
implicit_context: The hypotheses impose independence within each row; no independence relationship between variables belonging to different rows is stated (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; structural anchor: row-wise list of independent variables).
The success probabilities need not be equal within a row, as they carry both indices N and i (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; structural anchor: p_{N,1}, ..., p_{N,N}).

details: Row N contains exactly N Bernoulli variables indexed i=1,...,N (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; structural anchor: the doubly indexed family X_{N,i}).
The theorem is not stated for one fixed iid sequence: both the variables and their probabilities may change with N (same location; anchor: the two indices on X_{N,i} and p_{N,i}).
The maximum individual success probability must vanish (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: max_i p_{N,i} → 0).
The sum of the success probabilities must approach λ (same location; anchor: ∑_i p_{N,i} → λ).
Both limiting assumptions are required jointly; neither alone is the stated theorem (same location; anchor: the paired displayed assumptions).

The limit is the full Poisson(λ) probability law defined by its point masses, rather than only a numerical parameter or moment assertion (PDF page 6, printed page 10; anchors: the preceding Poisson mass-function definition and Theorem 1.3.4's conclusion).
The relation is convergence in distribution of the unnormalized row sums (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: converges in distribution).

X_{N,i} are Bernoulli summands, p_{N,i} are their success probabilities, S_N is their row sum, and λ is both the limit of total success probability and the parameter of the limiting Poisson law (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchors: its opening, assumptions, and conclusion).

undebatable_constraints: The summands must be Bernoulli variables, retaining their two-point law rather than merely Bernoulli moments (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: Bernoulli random variables with parameters p_{N,i}).
Independence is required among the variables in each row (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: independent).
The row is triangular: row N contains the variables indexed i=1,...,N (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; structural anchor: X_{N,1}, ..., X_{N,N}).
The largest row probability tends to zero (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: max_i p_{N,i} → 0).
The sum of the row probabilities tends to the finite parameter λ (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: ∑_i p_{N,i} → λ).

The conclusion is convergence in distribution of the row sums, without centering or scaling, to the Poisson law with parameter λ (PDF page 6, printed page 10, Theorem 1.3.4; anchor: the concluding sentence).
The limiting Poisson law is the discrete law on k=0,1,2,... with mass e^{-λ}λ^k/k! (PDF page 6, printed page 10; anchor: the Poisson definition immediately preceding Theorem 1.3.4).

ambiguities.evidence: The source locator describes λ as finite, while the immediately preceding Poisson definition supplies the source's admissible parameter convention (PDF page 6, printed page 10; anchors: finite λ and the Poisson definition).
ambiguities.impact: A formalization should preserve the source's stated parameter range; it should not silently exclude or add the degenerate λ=0 case if the source's definition treats that endpoint differently.

contract_plain_english: For each N, take a row of N independent Bernoulli trials whose success probabilities may all differ. If every individual probability becomes negligible while the sum of the probabilities approaches a finite λ, then the number of successes in the row converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable with parameter λ, whose mass at k is e^{-λ}λ^k/k!.
